claim: Attack behaviour is stochastic (the time an attack takes is a random variable).
quote: As with failure rates, to properly model the intrusion process there is a need to also model the time between intrusions, often referred to as time to compromise (TTC)—the time spent by one or more attackers to successfully compromise a system.
issue: Holm fits statistical distributions to TTC, so it treats attack time as random; but the evidence is malware alarms across 261,757 enterprise systems (time between intrusions of a host), not the duration of one attacker's tactic.

claim: Holm's study supports timing tactics with exponential delays (the citation closes the sentence that justifies the exponential delay).
quote: Regarding RQ1, the results show that the log-normal distribution is best suited for modeling the number of intrusions of a computer system. The results are slightly different for RQ2, where the Pareto distribution is best fit for modeling the time to first intrusion and the log-normal distribution for modeling the time between intrusions.
locator: p. 14 printed (PDF p. 13), Sec. 7; the abstract calls the Poisson-process (exponential) assumption "unoptimal"
issue: Holm's finding is that the exponential (Poisson-process) assumption fits worse than log-normal and Pareto; cited in the sentence that justifies exponential delays, it reads as support for the very assumption it rejects. An examiner who knows Holm would flag it.
fix_text: Split the reasons: keep "because the timed transitions of a GSPN fire after exponential delays (Section~\ref{sec:petri-formalism})" as the reason for the shape, and make the citation carry only randomness, e.g. "... and the time an attack takes is random~\citep{holm2014, ...}"; or own the cost: "... although measured times to compromise fit log-normal and Pareto distributions better~\citep{holm2014}".
